defaultValue.description: Initially selected value for an uncontrolled Select. Omit it to start on the placeholder.

onValueChange.description: Fires with the newly selected value. Selection is committed on click, Enter, Space, or typeahead — not while arrowing through the list.

open.description: Controlled open state of the listbox. Only needed when something outside the Select has to open or close it.

defaultOpen.description: Whether the listbox starts open for an uncontrolled Select.

onOpenChange.description: Fires when the listbox opens or closes.

disabled.description: Whether the whole control is non-interactive. To disable one option, set disabled on that SelectItem instead.

required.description: Whether a value must be chosen before the form can be submitted. Sets aria-required on the trigger.

name.description: Form field name applied to the hidden native select, under which the value is submitted.

values.description: Left-to-right reading order.
Right-to-left reading order, which mirrors the content's alignment against the trigger.

dir.description: Reading direction. Inherited from an ambient direction provider when omitted.

subComponents.name: SelectTrigger
subComponents.description: The button that opens the listbox. Renders role combobox with aria-expanded, shows the current value, and draws its own chevron; it accepts a size of "default" or "sm". Give it an id — this is the element a Label's htmlFor must point at, and the element that carries aria-invalid.

subComponents.name: SelectValue
subComponents.description: The trigger's text: it renders the selected item's label automatically, or the placeholder while nothing is selected. Pass the empty-state text through its placeholder prop rather than as children.

subComponents.name: SelectContent
subComponents.description: The portalled listbox holding the options. Renders role listbox and provides its own scrolling viewport and scroll buttons. Defaults to position "item-aligned", which lines the selected item up over the trigger; switch to "popper" to anchor it below the trigger like a menu.

subComponents.name: SelectItem
subComponents.description: A single option, rendered as role option with a check indicator for the selected state. Requires a unique, non-empty value. Its children are normally the option's text, optionally with a leading icon or a trailing Badge; whenever they are not plain text, set textValue so typeahead and the value shown in the trigger stay meaningful.

subComponents.name: SelectGroup
subComponents.description: Groups related items under a SelectLabel. Renders role group and is labelled by the SelectLabel inside it, so assistive technology announces the group name alongside its options.

subComponents.name: SelectLabel
subComponents.description: A non-interactive heading naming a SelectGroup. It supplies the group's accessible name only when it sits inside a SelectGroup; used on its own it is decorative text. It is not the form field's label — that is a separate Label bound to the trigger.

subComponents.name: SelectSeparator
subComponents.description: A decorative divider between groups of options. Not focusable and skipped by keyboard navigation, so it must never carry meaning of its own.

composition.notes: Select takes exactly two children: a SelectTrigger and a SelectContent. SelectValue belongs inside the trigger; SelectItem, SelectGroup, SelectLabel, and SelectSeparator belong inside the content, with SelectLabel nested in the SelectGroup it names. shadcn renders the scrolling viewport and the scroll-up/scroll-down buttons inside SelectContent for you — those parts are exported but are not part of normal composition. The field's own Label lives outside the Select and points at the trigger's id.

keyboardInteractions.description: On the trigger, opens the listbox and moves focus to the first item. On an item, selects it, closes the listbox, and returns focus to the trigger.
On the trigger, opens the listbox with focus on the currently selected item. On an item, selects it and closes the listbox.
On the trigger, opens the listbox. Inside the listbox, moves focus to the next or previous enabled item without committing a selection.
Closes the listbox without changing the selection and returns focus to the trigger.

Typeahead: jumps to the first item whose text starts with what was typed. With the listbox closed, typing on the trigger changes the selected value directly, so items need meaningful text or an explicit textValue.
The trigger is the control's single tab stop. Options are reached with the arrow keys and typeahead while the listbox is open, never with Tab.

requiredAttributes.condition: on the SelectTrigger
requiredAttributes.description: The field's Label must reference the trigger with htmlFor. Pointing at the hidden native select instead leaves the focusable control unnamed.

requiredAttributes.condition: on the SelectTrigger when the field has failed validation
requiredAttributes.description: Set it on the trigger, which is the element the user focuses and shadcn styles from this attribute, and reference the error message with aria-describedby.

requiredAttributes.condition: on the SelectTrigger when hint or error text qualifies the field
requiredAttributes.description: Reference the ids of that text so it is announced with the control.

accessibility.focusManagement: Focus starts on the trigger. Opening moves focus into the listbox, onto the selected item or the first item when nothing is selected, and contains it there; choosing an item or pressing Escape closes the listbox and returns focus to the trigger. Unlike RadioGroup, selection does not follow focus — arrow keys only move the highlight until Enter, Space, or a click commits.
accessibility.notes: The roles are split across the parts: trigger is combobox with aria-expanded and aria-controls, content is listbox, item is option, and SelectGroup is a group labelled by its SelectLabel. Radix keeps a hidden native select in sync for form submission; it is aria-hidden, so never label, style, or target it. The listbox renders in a portal, so it escapes ancestor overflow but also any ancestor that assumed it could clip its children.

constraints.context: One value from a list of roughly six or more known options
constraints.rule: Use Select

constraints.context: Two to five options that fit on screen
constraints.rule: Use RadioGroup instead of Select

constraints.context: The user may pick more than one value
constraints.rule: Use Checkboxes or a dedicated multi-select instead of Select

constraints.context: A list long enough that the user would want to type to narrow it, or a value that may not be in the list
constraints.rule: Use a combobox instead of Select

constraints.context: Every SelectItem
constraints.rule: Give it a unique, non-empty value — the empty string is how Radix represents nothing selected, so an item using it can never be shown as the selection

constraints.context: An empty, "None", or "All" choice
constraints.rule: Express the empty state with the SelectValue placeholder, or add an item with a real value such as "none" — never an item with an empty value

constraints.context: Any Select
constraints.rule: Associate a visible Label with the SelectTrigger's id

constraints.context: Items whose content is not plain text, such as icons, badges, or two-line rows
constraints.rule: Set textValue on the item so typeahead and the value rendered in the trigger stay meaningful

constraints.context: Options that fall into categories
constraints.rule: Wrap each category in a SelectGroup with a SelectLabel inside it rather than faking headings with disabled items

constraints.context: A trigger that shows no chosen value yet
constraints.rule: Give SelectValue a placeholder that names the field's subject, not a bare "Select..."

alert.name: Alert
alert.description: A static, in-page callout that draws attention to a short message without interrupting the flow. Renders a div with a hardcoded role="alert" and lays out an optional icon, a title, a description, and an optional action on a grid. Alert is presentational: it has no open state, no dismiss affordance, and no portal, and it stays wherever you place it in the document.
alert.whenToUse: Use for a persistent message that belongs to a region of the page: a form-level error summary above the submit button, a plan-limit warning on a settings panel, an informational note explaining a feature. Reach for Alert when the message must stay on screen for as long as the condition holds and the user should be able to re-read it after looking away.
alert.whenNotToUse: Do not use for a transient confirmation of something the user just did — Sonner clears itself, Alert does not. Do not use to block a workflow or demand a decision; that is AlertDialog. Do not use it as a generic bordered container for arbitrary content; that is Card. Do not use it for a short status label attached to a row or item; that is Badge.

values.description: Neutral callout on the card surface. Covers informational and warning messages; carry the meaning in the icon and the title text rather than in colour.
Errors and failures. Tints the title, the icon, and the description with the destructive token.

variant.description: Visual treatment. shadcn ships only these two variants — there is no success or warning variant — so other tones are built by adding utility classes through className.

className.description: Additional CSS classes. This is the sanctioned way to produce tones shadcn does not ship a variant for (for example bg-amber-50 dark:bg-amber-950 for a warning) and to constrain the alert's width; the component is w-full and fills its parent.

requiredAttributes.condition: when the Alert is part of the initial page render rather than appearing in response to an event
requiredAttributes.description: Override the built-in role with role="status" or role="note". role="alert" is an assertive live region that interrupts whatever the screen reader is currently saying — correct for an error that appears after a failed submit, wrong for a callout that was always on the page. The component spreads incoming props after its own role, so the value you pass wins.

requiredAttributes.condition: on the decorative icon passed as a direct child of Alert
requiredAttributes.description: Mark the icon aria-hidden="true". It restates what the title already says, and the alert is announced as one block of text, so an unnamed or named icon only adds noise at the front of the message.

requiredAttributes.condition: only when the alert's own text does not identify what it refers to
requiredAttributes.description: Alert takes its accessible name from its content, so a label is normally unnecessary. Prefer rewriting the title to name the subject over bolting on a label that screen-reader users hear and sighted users do not.

keyboardInteractions.description: Moves focus to interactive controls inside the alert, such as the Button in AlertAction. The Alert container itself is not focusable and defines no keyboard behaviour of its own.

accessibility.focusManagement: Alert never moves, traps, or restores focus. When one appears after a failed submit, leave focus where the user put it and let role="alert" do the announcing; move focus into the alert only when the user's next action genuinely lives there.
accessibility.notes: role="alert" is hardcoded on the root element, which makes every Alert an assertive, atomic live region. Reserve that for messages the user must hear immediately and downgrade the rest with an explicit role. AlertTitle and AlertDescription are plain divs, not headings, and are not wired to the container with aria-labelledby or aria-describedby — the whole alert is announced as a single run of text, so write the title and description to read well when concatenated.

subComponents.name: AlertTitle
subComponents.description: The one-line headline of the alert. Rendered as a div with a medium font weight — not a heading — and moved into the second grid column when an icon is present. Write it as the message itself, not a category label: "Your trial ends in 3 days" rather than "Warning".

subComponents.name: AlertDescription
subComponents.description: Supporting detail below the title, in muted foreground. Styled to handle paragraphs and inline links, so it can hold more than a single string when the message needs to explain a consequence or point at documentation.

subComponents.name: AlertAction
subComponents.description: An absolutely positioned slot in the top-right corner of the alert holding a single action control, usually an outline or ghost Button. Its presence adds right padding to the alert so the title and description never run underneath it. AlertAction is the container, not the control.

composition.notes: Order the children as icon, AlertTitle, AlertDescription, AlertAction. The grid switches to a two-column layout only when a direct svg child is present, and it spans that icon across both text rows, so pass at most one icon and pass it as a direct child of Alert rather than nesting it inside the title. AlertAction is positioned absolutely wherever it appears in the markup; keep it last so the DOM order still matches the reading order. Alert has no close button and no dismiss state — if the message should go away on its own, it is a toast, not an alert.

constraints.context: A persistent in-page message tied to a region, a form, or a record
constraints.rule: Use Alert

constraints.context: A transient confirmation of an action the user just completed
constraints.rule: Use Sonner instead of Alert, so the message clears itself

constraints.context: A message that must block the workflow until the user chooses
constraints.rule: Use AlertDialog instead of Alert

constraints.context: An Alert present in the initial render rather than appearing in response to an event
constraints.rule: Pass role="status" or role="note" to override the built-in role="alert", so a static callout does not interrupt the screen reader

constraints.context: An error or failure message
constraints.rule: Use variant="destructive"

constraints.context: Success and warning states, for which shadcn ships no variant
constraints.rule: Add the tone with utility classes on className and keep the meaning in the title text and the icon; do not convey the state through colour alone

constraints.context: Any alert
constraints.rule: Include an AlertTitle so the message has a scannable headline

constraints.context: The decorative icon passed as a direct child of Alert
constraints.rule: Mark it aria-hidden="true"; it duplicates the title

constraints.context: Making the whole alert clickable
constraints.rule: Put a real Button inside AlertAction instead of attaching a click handler to the Alert container

constraints.context: More than one interactive control in a single alert
constraints.rule: Reduce to one action in AlertAction, or move the decision into an AlertDialog; the action slot is a fixed corner position sized for a single control

progress.name: Progress
progress.description: A determinate progress bar built on Radix UI Progress. Renders a track with role="progressbar" and an indicator whose horizontal offset is driven by the value prop, and publishes aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax, and aria-valuetext automatically. The shadcn wrapper renders both the track and the indicator itself and exports no sub-components.
progress.whenToUse: Use when completion can be expressed as a number the user can watch move: a file upload, a multi-step form, a quota filling up, an import job reporting processed records. Progress earns its place when quantifying the remaining work tells the user something a spinner cannot.
progress.whenNotToUse: Do not use when you cannot compute a percentage — an operation of unknown length needs a Spinner, and a page or panel waiting on its content needs a Skeleton. Do not use it as a gauge for a static quantity: a battery level, a score, or a disk-usage readout is a meter, not progress, and must not claim role="progressbar". Do not use it as a decorative rule or as the connector line in a stepper.

value.description: How much of the task is complete, on a 0–100 scale. Radix treats a missing or null value as indeterminate and drops aria-valuenow, but the shadcn wrapper computes the indicator offset as translateX(-${100 - (value || 0)}%), so omitting value paints a permanently empty track instead of an indeterminate animation. Always pass a number; when the duration is unknown, use Spinner instead.

max.description: Upper bound of value, published as aria-valuemax. Radix falls back to 100 when max is absent or not greater than zero. Note that the shipped indicator transform is hardcoded to a 0–100 scale: setting max to anything else keeps the ARIA values correct while rendering the bar at the wrong width. Normalise your value to a percentage before passing it, or edit the transform in progress.tsx.

getValueLabel.description: (value, max) => string. Produces the aria-valuetext announced in place of the raw number; Radix's default returns a rounded percentage. Override it when a percentage is not the useful unit — "3 of 8 files", "about 2 minutes left" — so the announcement matches whatever is written next to the bar.

className.description: Additional CSS classes. Use it to constrain the width (the track is w-full and fills its parent) and to override the shipped track height. Colour comes from the primary and muted tokens; restyling the indicator means editing progress.tsx, as the indicator is not reachable through props.

requiredAttributes.condition: when no visible text names the progress bar
requiredAttributes.description: Radix supplies the value attributes but never a name. Without aria-label or aria-labelledby the bar is announced as a bare percentage with no indication of what is progressing.

requiredAttributes.condition: when a visible label or heading already names the progress bar
requiredAttributes.description: Reference the id of that visible text rather than duplicating it in aria-label; shadcn's own example wires this up with the Field component. Use one or the other, never both.

requiredAttributes.condition: always — applied automatically, never by hand
requiredAttributes.description: Radix derives aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax, and aria-valuetext from value, max, and getValueLabel. A hand-written value disagrees with the rendered indicator the moment state changes, so change the value prop instead.

accessibility.focusManagement: Progress is not focusable and takes no part in the tab order. When the operation finishes and the bar is replaced, move focus deliberately to whatever the user should do next rather than letting it fall to the body.
accessibility.notes: Radix sets data-state to loading, complete, or indeterminate, which is available for styling. Screen readers do not reliably re-announce a progressbar as its value changes, and they do not announce completion — do not rely on the bar alone to report that a task finished; say so in a polite live region or in visible copy. If the bar reports a static quantity rather than an operation in flight, role="meter" is the correct role and this is the wrong component.

composition.notes: Progress renders the Radix Root and Indicator itself and exports no sub-components, so nothing goes inside it. Build the label and the numeric readout as siblings — shadcn's documented example composes Progress with Field for exactly this — and point aria-labelledby at the visible label.

constraints.context: An operation whose completion can be expressed as a percentage
constraints.rule: Use Progress with an explicit value

constraints.context: An operation of unknown duration
constraints.rule: Use Spinner instead of Progress; a progressbar with no value announces nothing useful and, as shipped, renders an empty track rather than an indeterminate animation

constraints.context: Any progress bar
constraints.rule: Give it an accessible name with aria-label, or with aria-labelledby pointing at the visible label

constraints.context: A value on a scale other than 0–100
constraints.rule: Normalise the value to a percentage before passing it; the shipped indicator transform ignores max

constraints.context: A static quantity such as a battery level, disk usage, or a score
constraints.rule: Use an element with role="meter" instead of Progress

constraints.context: Reporting that a task has finished
constraints.rule: Announce completion in a polite live region or in visible copy as well; a progressbar reaching its maximum is not reliably announced

constraints.context: Setting aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax, or aria-valuetext by hand
constraints.rule: Let Radix derive them from value, max, and getValueLabel

constraints.context: A unit the user cares about that is not a percentage
constraints.rule: Pass getValueLabel so the announced text matches the visible readout

skeleton.name: Skeleton
skeleton.description: A pulsing placeholder block that stands in for content that has not arrived yet. It is a single muted, rounded div with animate-pulse and no intrinsic size — you give it the shape of the content it replaces using utility classes. It carries no ARIA role and no loading semantics of its own; those belong to the region that contains it.
skeleton.whenToUse: Use when you already know the shape of the content that is loading and the wait is short enough that showing the layout reassures more than a spinner would: a card grid, the first page of a table, a profile header, a form being hydrated. Skeletons are most valuable when they hold the layout still so nothing jumps when the real content lands.
skeleton.whenNotToUse: Do not use for feedback on an action the user just triggered — a submitting button wants a Spinner inside it, not a placeholder where the control used to be. Do not use when real progress is measurable; that is Progress. Do not use for long or open-ended waits, where a repeating pulse becomes noise: show an explanatory empty or error state instead. Do not ship a skeleton whose dimensions differ from the content that replaces it.

className.description: Utility classes that give the placeholder its size and shape. The component ships with no width and no height, so a Skeleton with no className renders a zero-size element and is invisible. Always pass at least a height and a width (h-4 w-[250px]), add rounded-full for avatars and other circles, and match the values to the real content so the layout does not shift on swap.

aria-hidden.description: Removes the placeholder from the accessibility tree. Skeletons carry no information — a screen reader walking a tree of empty divs learns nothing — so hide them and announce the loading state once on the containing region instead. The component does not set this for you.

requiredAttributes.condition: on every Skeleton
requiredAttributes.description: Set aria-hidden="true" so assistive technology does not walk a tree of empty placeholder elements. The shipped component sets no role and no ARIA attributes of any kind.

requiredAttributes.condition: on the container that will hold the loaded content
requiredAttributes.description: Set aria-busy="true" while the placeholders are showing and remove it when the real content renders, so assistive technology knows the region is incomplete rather than empty.

requiredAttributes.condition: on the region that reports the loading state
requiredAttributes.description: Announce the transition once — a polite live region, or a visually hidden element with role="status" containing text such as "Loading results", swapped for the count when the data arrives. Skeletons announce nothing themselves.

accessibility.focusManagement: Skeletons are not focusable and must not be made focusable. If a placeholder replaces a control the user had focused, focus is dropped to the body when the skeleton mounts — prefer disabling the control in place over swapping it for a skeleton, and restore focus deliberately when the content arrives.
accessibility.notes: The pulse comes from Tailwind's animate-pulse, which runs regardless of the user's motion preference. Add motion-reduce:animate-none (or scope the animation in CSS) so users who have asked for reduced motion get a static placeholder. Because the component is a bare div, everything about how the loading state is communicated — the busy state, the announcement, the eventual result — is the caller's responsibility.

composition.notes: Skeleton has no sub-components. Build a placeholder by composing several Skeletons inside the same layout primitives the real content uses, so the two are structurally interchangeable and the swap causes no reflow. shadcn documents this pattern for avatars, cards, text runs, forms, and tables.

constraints.context: Content whose layout is known and will arrive shortly
constraints.rule: Use Skeleton shaped like the content it replaces

constraints.context: Any Skeleton
constraints.rule: Pass explicit size classes on className; the component has no intrinsic dimensions and renders invisibly without them

constraints.context: A loading region built from skeletons
constraints.rule: Mark the skeletons aria-hidden="true" and announce the loading state once on the containing region

constraints.context: A placeholder whose dimensions do not match the content that replaces it
constraints.rule: Match the skeleton to the real layout so the page does not shift when content lands

constraints.context: Users who have requested reduced motion
constraints.rule: Suppress the pulse with motion-reduce:animate-none; animate-pulse does not honour the preference on its own

constraints.context: Feedback for an action the user just triggered, such as a submitting button
constraints.rule: Put a Spinner inside the control instead of replacing it with a Skeleton

constraints.context: A load that fails or runs indefinitely
constraints.rule: Replace the skeletons with an explanatory empty or error state rather than pulsing forever

constraints.context: A control that the user may have focused
constraints.rule: Disable it in place rather than swapping it for a Skeleton, so focus is not dropped to the body

spinner.name: Spinner
spinner.description: An indeterminate loading indicator. It is a single lucide icon — Loader2Icon as shipped — rendered with animate-spin and a hardcoded role="status" and aria-label="Loading". There are no variants and no size prop: size and colour come from utility classes, and the icon is changed by editing the component rather than through a prop.
spinner.whenToUse: Use for a wait whose length you cannot predict and whose shape you cannot draw: a button that has just submitted, a field validating against the server, an input group fetching suggestions, a small region refreshing in place. Spinner works best inside or beside the control that started the work, so the indicator is where the user is already looking.
spinner.whenNotToUse: Do not use when completion is measurable — that is Progress. Do not use for the first paint of a page or panel whose layout you already know; Skeleton holds the layout and reads as faster. Do not scatter several spinners across one view: one indicator per in-flight operation, placed at the operation.

className.description: Utility classes. Size the spinner with size-* — it ships at size-4 — and colour it with a text-* class. The icon draws with currentColor, so by default it inherits the colour of whatever it sits inside, which is usually what you want inside a Button or Badge.

aria-label.description: Accessible name of the indicator. The component sets "Loading" and spreads incoming props afterwards, so passing aria-label replaces it. Make it specific when more than one thing on the page can be loading ("Loading search results"), and localise it — the built-in string is English and is not translated.

aria-hidden.description: Removes the spinner from the accessibility tree. Set it to true whenever the surrounding control already announces the state — a Button whose accessible name changes to "Saving…", or a region with its own role="status" — so the wait is announced once rather than twice.

requiredAttributes.condition: when the built-in "Loading" is ambiguous, or the interface is not in English
requiredAttributes.description: Replace the hardcoded English default with a localised, specific name. The component supplies a name, so the requirement is already met by default — but the default is neither translated nor scoped to what is actually loading.

requiredAttributes.condition: when the spinner sits inside a control or region that already announces the loading state
requiredAttributes.description: Set aria-hidden="true" so the spinner's role="status" does not compete with the announcement you already make on the control. Two live regions describing the same wait is worse than one.

accessibility.focusManagement: Spinner is not focusable and takes no part in the tab order. When it appears inside a Button, keep the Button mounted and set disabled rather than unmounting or replacing it, so focus is not dropped to the body while the operation runs.
accessibility.notes: role="status" makes the icon a polite live region, but its content never changes after mount, and screen readers vary in whether they announce a live region that is itself inserted into the DOM. Do not rely on the spinner alone to tell a screen-reader user that work has started: change the control's accessible name ("Save" to "Saving…"), set aria-busy on the region, or announce the state in a live region you own — and mark the spinner aria-hidden so it does not duplicate that. animate-spin does not honour prefers-reduced-motion, so a continuously rotating indicator keeps rotating for users who have asked for less motion.

composition.notes: Spinner has no sub-components — it is the thing that gets composed. shadcn documents it inside Button, Badge, InputGroup, and Empty; place it before the label with data-icon="inline-start" or after it with data-icon="inline-end" to control which side it sits on. To use a different icon, swap the lucide import in spinner.tsx; there is no icon prop and no size prop.

constraints.context: An operation whose duration cannot be predicted
constraints.rule: Use Spinner

constraints.context: An operation whose completion can be quantified
constraints.rule: Use Progress instead of Spinner

constraints.context: The first load of a page or panel whose layout is known
constraints.rule: Use Skeleton instead of Spinner so the layout does not shift when content arrives

constraints.context: A button that has triggered an async action
constraints.rule: Keep the Button mounted and disabled with the Spinner inside it, rather than unmounting or replacing the control

constraints.context: A spinner inside a control that already announces its own loading state
constraints.rule: Set aria-hidden="true" on the Spinner so the state is announced once

constraints.context: A spinner that is the only signal that work has started
constraints.rule: Also change the control's accessible name or set aria-busy on the region; a static role="status" element is not reliably announced when it is inserted into the DOM

constraints.context: An interface that is not in English
constraints.rule: Pass a localised aria-label; the built-in "Loading" string is hardcoded and untranslated

constraints.context: Users who have requested reduced motion
constraints.rule: Stop or slow the rotation; animate-spin runs regardless of the prefers-reduced-motion setting

constraints.context: Several concurrent operations in one view
constraints.rule: Show one spinner per in-flight operation, positioned at that operation, rather than a single global indicator or a field of spinners

sonner.name: Sonner
sonner.description: The toast system shadcn ships, wrapping the sonner library. The registry item installs exactly one component — Toaster — which you mount once at the root of the app and theme through next-themes. Individual toasts are not written as JSX: you call toast() from the sonner package anywhere in your code and the mounted Toaster renders, stacks, and expires them. A toast's title, description, icon, action, and cancel button are all options on that call.
sonner.whenToUse: Use to confirm the outcome of something the user just did, when the message is short, needs no response, and can be missed without consequence: "Event created", "Copied to clipboard", "Changes saved". Use toast.promise for an async action that should report loading and then success or failure from a single call site.
sonner.whenNotToUse: Do not use for anything the user must read or act on. A toast disappears on a timer, is announced only politely, and sits outside the tab order — an error that blocks progress belongs in an Alert beside the thing that failed, and a decision belongs in an AlertDialog. Do not use it for field-level validation errors; put those on the field. Do not narrate a process with a run of toasts; only a few are visible at a time and the rest collapse.

values.description: The default. Least intrusive on desktop, and furthest from primary content.
Reads as a status line along the bottom edge. Works well in mobile-first layouts where the thumb is already there.
Keeps toasts clear of a right-hand rail, inspector, or chat launcher.
Common when the primary actions live in the top bar, so feedback appears near the control that produced it.
The most noticeable placement. Use it when toasts carry information users should not miss, and nothing else is anchored to the top.
Useful in RTL layouts, or when the bottom of the viewport is occupied by fixed chrome.

position.description: Where the stack is anchored in the viewport. It also determines the default swipe-to-dismiss directions. Individual toasts can override it per call, but a stable position is easier to learn.

values.description: Follows the OS colour scheme. This is what the shadcn wrapper passes when next-themes has no explicit preference.
Force the light surface regardless of the app theme.
Force the dark surface regardless of the app theme.

theme.description: Colour scheme of the toasts. The shadcn wrapper already reads the app theme from next-themes and passes it down, so you normally leave this alone; because props are spread last, passing it explicitly overrides the wired-up theme and can desynchronise toasts from the rest of the UI.

richColors.description: Tints success, error, warning, and info toasts with their semantic colours instead of the neutral popover surface. The built-in icons already distinguish the types, so treat this as emphasis rather than as the signal — and check the tinted surfaces for contrast in both themes before enabling it.

closeButton.description: Renders a dismiss button on every toast. Turn it on when toasts carry actions or text that takes longer than the duration to read; without it a toast can only be dismissed by swiping or by waiting it out.

expand.description: Shows the stack expanded rather than collapsed. By default only the front toast is fully visible and the stack expands on hover or when the notification hotkey is pressed.

visibleToasts.description: How many toasts are rendered at once; the rest queue behind them. Raising it makes the stack harder to scan and pushes more content over the page, so prefer fixing the code that emits a flood of toasts.

duration.description: Milliseconds a toast stays on screen before auto-dismissing, applied to every toast unless a call overrides it. Four seconds is not enough time to read a message, decide, and act, so raise it for any toast that carries an action.

offset.description: Distance from the viewport edge. Accepts one value or an object of top/right/bottom/left. Increase it when fixed chrome — a bottom bar, a consent banner, a floating action button — would otherwise sit under the toasts.

mobileOffset.description: Offset applied at mobile widths, where a large inset wastes scarce vertical space. Set it alongside offset whenever you change the desktop value.

values.description: Left-to-right. The default.
Right-to-left, for Arabic, Hebrew, and other RTL locales.
Reads the direction from the document at render time. Prefer this in apps that switch locales at runtime.

dir.description: Text direction of the toast list. It also affects which swipe directions dismiss a toast, so set it rather than relying on CSS alone in bidirectional interfaces.

hotkey.description: Key combination that expands the stack and moves focus into the notification region. This is the only keyboard route to a toast, and its human-readable form is appended to the region's accessible name ("Notifications alt+T"), so changing it changes what screen readers announce.

invert.description: Inverts toast colours against the current theme so they read as the opposite surface. Use it sparingly: it breaks the visual relationship between the toast and the rest of the interface, and it interacts badly with richColors.

icons.description: Map of toast type to the node rendered as its icon — success, info, warning, error, and loading. The shadcn wrapper already fills all five with lucide icons and animates the loading one; override it only to match a different icon set, and keep all five so the types stay distinguishable.

toastOptions.description: Defaults applied to every toast: duration, className and classNames, closeButton, style, and the other per-toast options. It is spread onto the underlying Toaster after the wrapper's own toastOptions, so passing it replaces rather than merges with whatever the shipped component set.

containerAriaLabel.description: Accessible name of the notification region, before the hotkey label is appended to it. The default is English; localise it in any non-English interface.

className.description: Classes applied to the toast list element. The shipped wrapper already sets "toaster group" on it, and because props are spread last, passing className replaces that rather than adding to it. To style individual toasts, use toastOptions.classNames.

requiredAttributes.condition: always — applied by sonner to the notification region
requiredAttributes.description: Sonner puts aria-live="polite", aria-relevant="additions text", and aria-atomic="false" on the wrapping region and leaves the individual toasts without any role. Every toast — including error toasts — is therefore announced politely, after whatever the screen reader is currently saying. There is no assertive path; if a message must interrupt, it should not be a toast.

requiredAttributes.condition: when the interface is not in English
requiredAttributes.description: Pass containerAriaLabel to localise the region's name, or customAriaLabel to replace the whole string including the hotkey suffix. The default is "Notifications" with the hotkey label appended.

keyboardInteractions.description: The default hotkey. Expands the stack and moves focus into the toast list. Toasts are deliberately outside the normal tab order, so this is the only way to reach one from the keyboard.
Once focus is inside the region, moves through the toasts and their action, cancel, and close buttons, then leaves the region and returns to the document.
Collapses the expanded stack while focus is inside the region. It does not dismiss the toasts.
Activates the focused action, cancel, or close button.
Activates the focused action, cancel, or close button.

accessibility.focusManagement: Toasts never take focus when they appear — that is the point of the pattern, and it is why they must not carry anything essential. Focus enters the region only through the hotkey, and sonner restores focus to the previously focused element when focus leaves the region or the region unmounts. A toast can auto-dismiss while a keyboard user is still tabbing through it, so never put the only copy of an action inside one.
accessibility.notes: Individual toasts carry no role of their own — not role="alert", not role="status" — and are announced only because they are inserted into the wrapping polite live region. That makes toasts unsuitable for urgent content: an error that must interrupt belongs in an Alert next to the failure, or in an AlertDialog if a decision is needed. Because toasts sit outside the tab order, a keyboard user who does not know the hotkey cannot reach an action inside one before it expires. Duration is an accessibility constraint, not a style preference: WCAG SC 2.2.1 (Timing Adjustable) covers content that disappears on a timer, so raise duration and enable closeButton for anything actionable.

composition.notes: There are no sub-components. A toast's anatomy — type icon, title, description, action button, cancel button, and the optional close button — is data passed to the toast() call, not JSX you nest. The surface is toast(title, options) plus toast.success, toast.info, toast.warning, toast.error, toast.loading, toast.message, toast.promise, toast.custom, and toast.dismiss(id), imported from the sonner package rather than from your components directory; the registry item's only export is Toaster. The rendered structure is Toaster > notification region > toast list > toast, and none of those levels is addressable as a component. Mount exactly one Toaster in the root layout, outside any conditionally rendered subtree, and every toast() call in the app renders into it.

constraints.context: Confirming a short, non-blocking outcome of an action the user just took
constraints.rule: Use Sonner

constraints.context: Anywhere in the application
constraints.rule: Mount exactly one Toaster, in the root layout; a second one splits the queue and produces duplicate announcements

constraints.context: An error the user must act on, or information they must not miss
constraints.rule: Use an Alert beside the thing that failed instead of a toast; toasts auto-dismiss, are announced only politely, and sit outside the tab order

constraints.context: A message that requires a decision before the user can continue
constraints.rule: Use AlertDialog instead of a toast

constraints.context: Validation errors on a specific form field
constraints.rule: Render the error on the field rather than in a toast

constraints.context: A toast that carries an action such as Undo
constraints.rule: Raise duration, enable closeButton, and provide a permanent way to perform the same action elsewhere; a keyboard or screen-reader user may never reach the toast before it expires

constraints.context: An async operation reported from a single call site
constraints.rule: Use toast.promise so one toast moves through loading, success, and error rather than stacking three

constraints.context: Signalling the kind of a toast
constraints.rule: Call the typed helper (toast.success, toast.error, toast.warning, toast.info) so the correct icon renders; do not rely on richColors alone to carry the meaning

constraints.context: An interface that is not in English
constraints.rule: Pass containerAriaLabel so the notification region is named in the user's language

constraints.context: A sequence of steps the user should be able to review
constraints.rule: Write the outcome into the page — a log, a status column, an Alert — instead of emitting a run of toasts that expire unread

interactive.name: Interactive
interactive.description: Receives pointer or keyboard activation: buttons, inputs, menu items, and trigger/action/cancel sub-components. Category-based composition rules select by this instead of enumerating ids.

overlay.name: Overlay
overlay.description: Renders content in a layer above the page with its own focus and dismiss semantics: dialogs, alert dialogs, dropdown menus.

form.name: Form
form.description: Form structure and controls: field wrappers, labels, descriptions, validation messages, and the inputs they name.

layout.name: Layout
layout.description: Arranges, bounds, or separates other content without presenting content of its own: separators, scroll containers, ratio boxes, and structural wrappers.

content.name: Content
content.description: Presents content directly — text, media, labels, and identity: avatars and their images and fallbacks, disclosure panels, captions.

feedback.name: Feedback
feedback.description: Communicates system state to the user: alerts, progress, loading placeholders, and transient notifications.

navigation.name: Navigation
navigation.description: Moves the user between views or between panels of one view: tabs, breadcrumbs, and pagination.

patterns.name: Destructive Action Confirmation
patterns.description: A confirmation flow for actions that are irreversible or have significant consequences, using AlertDialog to require explicit user acknowledgment.
patterns.intent: Prevent accidental data loss or irreversible state changes by requiring the user to explicitly confirm before proceeding.
patterns.context: Use whenever an action cannot be undone: deleting a record, removing a team member, clearing form data, revoking access, or any operation the user might regret if triggered accidentally.
patterns.guidance: Use AlertDialog, not Dialog, for destructive confirmations. The trigger should clearly indicate the destructive nature of the action. Inside the AlertDialog, provide a clear title stating what will happen, a description of the consequences, and two actions: a cancel option and a confirm option. The confirm button MUST use the destructive variant. Place the cancel action before the confirm action in the footer. The description should state specifically what will be affected (e.g., 'This will permanently delete 3 projects and all associated data').

patterns.name: Form Field Layout
patterns.description: Standard arrangement of form controls within a Card container, providing consistent structure for data entry interfaces.
patterns.intent: Give forms a consistent visual structure that groups related inputs, separates them from surrounding content, and provides clear hierarchy through Card sub-components.
patterns.context: Use for settings panels, profile editors, checkout flows, or any interface where the user enters structured data across multiple fields.
patterns.guidance: Wrap the form in a Card. Use CardHeader with CardTitle and CardDescription to introduce the form's purpose. Place inputs inside CardContent with consistent vertical spacing (space-y-4 or equivalent). Group related fields together. Place primary actions (submit, save) in CardFooter. Labels should be associated with inputs for accessibility. Required fields should be visually indicated.

patterns.name: Contextual Actions Menu
patterns.description: A pattern for exposing a set of context-sensitive actions through a dropdown menu triggered by an icon button.
patterns.intent: Keep interfaces clean by collecting secondary or overflow actions behind a single trigger, while maintaining discoverability through a familiar interaction pattern.
patterns.context: Use for row-level actions in tables or lists, overflow menus in toolbars, or any place where multiple actions apply to a single item but showing all of them inline would be visually noisy.
patterns.guidance: Use a Button with the ghost variant and icon size as the DropdownMenuTrigger. A vertical ellipsis icon is the conventional trigger for contextual menus. Group related actions with DropdownMenuGroup and separate groups with DropdownMenuSeparator. Place destructive actions (delete, remove) at the end of the menu, visually distinguished. Include keyboard shortcuts in DropdownMenuItem when available.

patterns.name: Data Table with Row Actions
patterns.description: An enterprise data table that presents records with a sortable header, a status column, and a trailing column of per-row actions — including destructive ones routed through a confirmation. Composes the Table primitives with Badge for status, a DropdownMenu (via the contextual-actions-menu pattern) for the actions column, and AlertDialog (via the destructive-action-confirmation pattern) for destructive actions.
patterns.intent: Let users scan and act on a list of records — reviewing each row's status and reaching its actions — without sacrificing the semantics, keyboard access, or safety guarantees that the underlying components provide.
patterns.context: Use for access-management and administrative surfaces: a members table, a users-and-roles list, an API-keys table, or any view where each row is an entity with a status and a set of actions, some of which (remove, revoke access) are destructive.
patterns.guidance: Build the table from the Table primitives: a TableHeader row of TableHead cells, a TableBody of one TableRow per record, and a TableCaption (or aria-label) naming the table. Make sortable columns real controls — render a ghost Button inside the TableHead and set aria-sort on that TableHead to ascending, descending, or none, with only one column sorted at a time. Render the status column with a Badge whose variant reflects state (for example default or secondary for active and pending, destructive for suspended or revoked); because Badge is presentational, keep the status readable as text so it is announced by assistive technology, not conveyed by color alone. Put per-row actions in a trailing TableCell as a contextual-actions-menu: a ghost icon Button (a vertical ellipsis) as the DropdownMenuTrigger opening a DropdownMenu of actions, with an aria-label on the trigger. Route every destructive row action — remove, revoke access — through the destructive-action-confirmation pattern using AlertDialog, never Dialog, so the action cannot be dismissed by accident; the AlertDialogDescription should name the specific record affected (for example 'This revokes Jordan Lee's access to the Acme workspace'). Do not make the entire TableRow a single clickable target while it also contains its own action controls — that is the nested-interactive-elements anti-pattern, which produces ambiguous click targets and unpredictable behavior for keyboard and screen-reader users; if rows need a primary navigation, expose it as a distinct link or cell control rather than wrapping the row.

antiPatterns.name: Using Dialog for Destructive Confirmations
antiPatterns.description: Using the dismissible Dialog component instead of AlertDialog when confirming a destructive or irreversible action.
antiPatterns.reason: Dialog can be dismissed by clicking the overlay or pressing Escape, which means a user can accidentally bypass the confirmation without making a conscious choice. AlertDialog forces the user to select an explicit action (confirm or cancel), providing a stronger safeguard against accidental destructive operations. This distinction also matters for accessibility: screen readers announce AlertDialog with greater urgency.

antiPatterns.name: Nesting Interactive Elements
antiPatterns.description: Placing a clickable or focusable element (Button, Link, Input) inside another clickable element (a clickable Card, a Button, or a Link).
antiPatterns.reason: Nested interactive elements create ambiguous click targets and are a significant accessibility violation. Screen readers cannot determine user intent when interactive elements are nested, and the resulting behavior varies unpredictably across browsers. The outer element may intercept clicks intended for the inner element, or both may fire, leading to unexpected navigation or duplicate actions.

antiPatterns.name: Using a Styled Div as a Button
antiPatterns.description: Creating a clickable element by adding an onClick handler and visual styles to a <div> or <span> instead of using the Button component or a native <button> element.
antiPatterns.reason: A styled div lacks keyboard accessibility (not focusable by default, does not respond to Enter or Space), is not announced as a button by screen readers, and does not participate in form submission. The Button component handles all of these concerns. Using a div requires manually re-implementing focus management, keyboard handling, and ARIA attributes — work that is error-prone and already solved by the component.

intents.name: Destructive action
intents.description: The requested UI performs an irreversible or high-consequence operation: deleting records or accounts, revoking access, removing members.

intents.name: Record collection
intents.description: Surfaces that present many records of the same kind — support tickets, orders, members — for scanning and action. Records share uniform fields, so the collection renders as a semantic data table built from the Table primitives; status stays readable as text (badges are appropriate, color is never the only signal). Per-row actions and destructive confirmations follow the data-table-with-row-actions pattern as guidance until the dropdown-menu item vocabulary is specified.

intents.name: Structured input
intents.description: The requested UI collects structured values and commits them on an explicit action — a profile editor, a checkout step, a create-record form. Every control is named by a visible Label bound with htmlFor and id; placeholder text disappears on input and is never the accessible name. The control follows the shape of the answer: Input for a single line, Textarea for prose, RadioGroup for two to five exclusive options, Select for six or more, Checkbox for options that are independent of each other. Label, description, and error are associated through exactly one family per field — the react-hook-form Form parts, which generate the ids, or the Field parts, which require them to be written by hand — never a mix of the two.

intents.name: Preference settings
intents.description: A panel of settings that take effect the moment they change, with no Save step — notification preferences, workspace defaults, feature toggles. Each one is a Switch with a visible Label naming the setting rather than its current state ("Email notifications", never "On"); a Checkbox belongs here only when the change is staged for an explicit submit, and three or more choices are a RadioGroup or a Select, never a row of Switches. A toggle backed by a network write reflects the persisted result instead of an optimistic position that lies about the setting, and one whose effect is destructive or hard to reverse — disabling two-factor authentication — is confirmed before it applies.

intents.name: Record detail
intents.description: One entity presented for reading, with its actions attached — a member profile, an order summary, a ticket's detail pane. The record is grouped in a single Card and given hierarchy with headings and spacing rather than a Card nested inside another Card, and the Card itself is never the click target: actions are real controls placed inside it. Identity renders as an Avatar with a fallback that fills the box when the image never arrives and alt text carrying the name; thumbnails, cover art, and product photos are not identities and belong in an AspectRatio instead. Status reads as text — a Badge carries the tone, and a presence dot is restated in words, because a coloured dot has no accessible name. The record's secondary actions collect behind one named overflow trigger rather than crowding the header.

intents.name: Overlay task
intents.description: A focused task or detail the user completes without leaving the page behind it — editing a record, filtering a list, picking a date. The container follows how much of the user's attention the task must own: Popover for transient content anchored to the control that opened it, Dialog when the task deserves a focus trap, Sheet when it needs a full edge panel such as mobile navigation or a record editor. The panel names itself — a SheetTitle, visually hidden if the design shows none, and a PopoverContent wired by aria-labelledby to its title, which Radix Popover does not do for you. A trigger that is already a Button uses asChild rather than nesting a button inside a button. Confirming a destructive action is never one of these.

intents.name: Panel navigation
intents.description: One subject with several peer views the user switches between in place — Overview, Activity, and Settings on a record; Monthly and Yearly on a report. These are Tabs, not links: a view the user should be able to link to, bookmark, or reach with the back button is a route and belongs in navigation rather than in a tab set. Each trigger and its panel share a value unique within the set, the root supplies a defaultValue (or a controlled value) so one panel starts visible, and the tablist is given an accessible name when no visible heading names it. Unselected panels are unmounted, so anything that must be printable, comparable side by side, or reachable by find-in-page does not live in one.

intents.name: Wayfinding
intents.description: Controls that say where the user is and move them to another addressable position — the trail from the workspace root down to the record on screen, the pager beneath a long collection. Both render nav landmarks around a list of real anchors: every BreadcrumbLink and every PaginationLink carries an href, because an anchor without one is neither focusable nor announced as a link. Exactly one crumb is the BreadcrumbPage and exactly one pager link is active, so exactly one control carries aria-current="page". The ellipsis in either family is decorative and aria-hidden, never the affordance for reaching what it hides — the collapsed items need a real control with its own accessible name.

intents.name: Supplementary detail
intents.description: Detail the user may want but does not need in order to finish the task — what an icon-only button does, what an abbreviated column header means, the terms behind a one-line summary. A Tooltip holds a short phrase about the control it is attached to: it never receives focus, closes on click, and is absent entirely on touch, so it may hold no links or buttons and nothing required to complete the task, and it describes a control rather than naming it — an icon-only control still carries its own aria-label. Content the user can act on, or must read at their own pace, belongs in a named Popover or in an Accordion whose triggers hold no nested controls; a closed panel is unmounted, so nothing that must be reachable by find-in-page or print goes inside one.

intents.name: Status feedback
intents.description: The surface reports an outcome or a condition the user needs to know about — a save succeeded, an import partly failed, a workspace is over quota. Placement follows persistence and consequence: an Alert sits beside the thing it describes and stays there; a toast confirms something transient and clears itself, so it must never carry an error the user has to act on, a field's validation message, or information they cannot afford to miss. Errors take Alert's destructive variant, and because shadcn ships no success or warning variant, that meaning lives in the title text and the icon rather than in colour alone. A message that must block until the user chooses is not a status message but a confirmation.

intents.name: Loading state
intents.description: The surface stands in for work that has not finished — a panel fetching its first page, a form mid-submit, a file uploading. The indicator follows what is known about the work: a Skeleton shaped like the content when the layout is known, a Spinner when the duration cannot be predicted, and Progress only when completion is a real percentage, since a progressbar with no value announces nothing and renders an empty track. Skeletons are aria-hidden and the loading state is announced once on the region that contains them; a control the user has just activated stays mounted and disabled with the spinner inside it rather than being swapped for a placeholder that drops focus. Nothing pulses forever — a load that fails resolves to an explanatory error or empty state.

rules.rationale: Dialog can be dismissed by clicking the overlay or pressing Escape, so a user can bypass a destructive confirmation without making a conscious choice. AlertDialog forces an explicit confirm/cancel decision and is announced with greater urgency by screen readers.
A confirmation without an explicit cancel action and a title naming the consequence funnels the user toward the destructive action; the title is also required for aria-labelledby.
Nested interactive elements create ambiguous click targets and are an accessibility violation: screen readers cannot determine intent and click handling varies across browsers.

The trigger must present an accessible label: non-empty text somewhere under the trigger. Protocol projections lift the label from the trigger's subtree (preferring a label-bearing button; lifts are audited) — a trigger with no label text anywhere yields a control with no accessible name and an instance downstream emitters must refuse.

An alert dialog is a single focused interruption. Stacking another overlay (dialog, dropdown menu, another alert dialog) inside it breaks focus containment and dismiss semantics and buries the confirmation decision under a second layer.

The data-table-with-row-actions pattern: a record collection is built from the Table primitives, not prose or ad-hoc stacks. Records share uniform fields; a semantic table is how they stay scannable, sortable, and navigable by assistive technology.

The table's own constraints demand semantic structure: header cells as th within a TableHeader so screen readers can associate columns, and records inside a TableBody. A table without both is a grid of divs wearing table styling.

The data-table-with-row-actions pattern requires an accessible name via TableCaption or an aria-label. The pattern permits either; the contract can only govern the declarative form, so the caption is the enforceable floor — an aria-label alternative is legitimate but inexpressible in current rule types and remains guidance.

The sonner registry item exports exactly one component — Toaster — which is mounted once in the app's root layout; individual toasts are produced by toast() calls, never by JSX in a page. A surface that declares a Toaster mounts a second one, which splits the queue and announces every toast twice in the polite live region.

An alert takes its accessible name from its own content and is announced as one atomic run of text — AlertTitle is a plain div, not a heading, and is not wired to the container with aria-labelledby. An alert with no title, or an empty one, reaches the user as a bare description with no headline to scan.

Badge is presentational: it renders an inline element with no role, no accessible name of its own, and no aria-label in this vocabulary. A badge that carries only variant="destructive" reaches a screen-reader user as an empty element, so the record's status is conveyed by colour alone and the status column reads as blank.

TableHeader supplies only the thead; the column association comes from the cells inside it being named TableHead (th) elements. A header row built from TableCell, or one whose heads are empty, leaves every data cell announced with no column name — the user hears "Waiting on customer" with no way to tell which attribute it is.

A caption supplies the table's accessible name only if it says something. An empty TableCaption satisfies the presence requirement while leaving the table announced as an unnamed table, so a user arriving by rotor or landmark navigation is told there is a table of four columns and nothing about what the rows are.

Progress is determinate only: with no value the shipped indicator renders an empty track rather than an indeterminate animation, while Radix publishes role="progressbar" with no aria-valuenow — an import job that announces itself as a bar stuck at nothing. A wait you cannot quantify is a Spinner. The bar's accessible name is equally required but has no declarative form in these rule types.

Skeleton ships with no dimensions and no ARIA of its own. Without size classes it renders a zero-size element, so the loading state is invisible and the layout still jumps when content lands; left in the accessibility tree, a row of placeholders makes a screen reader walk empty divs that say nothing about the wait.

A skeleton stands in for content that has not arrived and is hidden from assistive technology. A control placed inside one stays in the tab order while being absent from the accessibility tree: the user tabs to something no screen reader can name. Keep the real control mounted and disabled instead of covering it.

The component hardcodes aria-label="Loading" — English, and identical for every spinner on the page. Where the table body, a filter, and a row action can each be in flight at once, three indicators announce the same word, and a localised interface announces an untranslated one.

The four overlay families differ mainly in how easily they can be abandoned. Popover is non-modal by default — focus and the pointer leave freely and Escape closes it — so a user can wander off with the confirmation unanswered; Sheet is a Radix Dialog and closes on Escape or an overlay click. Only AlertDialog blocks both exits and forces confirm or cancel.

DialogTitle is the only part that wires aria-labelledby onto the content. Without it Radix warns in development and ships a modal that traps focus while announcing nothing but "dialog" — the user is held inside a window whose purpose is never spoken. The title must carry its own text; a title whose label sits in a child projects as an empty name.

A Sheet is the same Radix Dialog primitive, so SheetTitle is what supplies its accessible name. On a small viewport the panel covers three quarters of the screen; announcing it only as "dialog" leaves the user trapped in unnamed content with no idea what they opened. A design with no visible title still renders SheetTitle, visually hidden — it is never dropped.

Popover is the one overlay with no ARIA wiring of its own: PopoverHeader, PopoverTitle and PopoverDescription are a div, a div and a p, not Radix parts, so rendering a title names nothing. PopoverContent still carries role="dialog", and a panel with no authored aria-labelledby is announced as a bare "dialog". A titled panel is the floor the contract can check; pointing aria-labelledby at that title's id remains the author's job.

TooltipContent takes short text only: it never receives focus, it closes on pointer-down and on click, and Radix ignores touch pointers outright, so anything composed inside it — a link, a button, a paragraph of instructions — is unreachable for keyboard and touch users. Content with no text of its own claims role="tooltip" and announces nothing at all.

Radix links the tooltip with aria-describedby, which is a description and not a name, and on touch the tooltip never opens at all. A control named only by its tooltip is therefore announced as an unnamed button to some users and as nothing whatsoever to others. The label must exist in the trigger's own subtree, where protocol projections lift it onto the control.

The contextual-actions trigger is a ghost icon button. With no text anywhere beneath it, every row's menu is announced identically as an unnamed button and the projection has nothing to lift into the trigger's aria-label — a screen reader user hears the same thing on every row and cannot tell which record's actions they opened.

shadcn defaults decorative to true, which renders role="none": a rule drawn to mark a real boundary between groups is then invisible to assistive technology, and the grouping exists for sighted users only. Ornament or structure is a decision, not a default — false where the divider carries the boundary, true where a heading or card edge already does.

A Card inside a Card draws two competing boundaries around one group and doubles the padding, so the inner group reads as a separate object and the outer surface loses its edge. Hierarchy within a card comes from headings and spacing: one bordered surface per group.

With neither value nor defaultValue Radix selects nothing: the tablist renders over a stack of hidden panels, so the surface shows a row of triggers above an empty region. A generated surface has no handler to pair with the controlled value, so defaultValue is the enforceable floor and must name the panel that opens first.

Radix pairs each trigger with its panel through a shared value: an unmatched trigger selects nothing, an unmatched panel never appears, and the trigger's aria-controls resolves to an element that does not exist. Requiring the tablist, at least one trigger and at least one panel is the floor; the one-to-one value match cannot be expressed here and stays guidance.

BreadcrumbList is an ol and every crumb must be an li within it, or the trail is announced as loose links with no position or count. The final crumb must be a BreadcrumbPage: it is what carries aria-current="page", and it renders a span rather than an anchor so the current page does not offer a link to itself. Exactly-one-and-last is not expressible; a minimum of one is the floor.

PaginationContent renders a ul, so a link dropped straight into it is not a list item: the pager loses its item count and its controls are announced as stray links inside a list. Every control, the ellipsis included, sits in its own PaginationItem.

AvatarImage mounts only once the image has actually loaded, so on a slow, blocked, or 404 URL the slot renders empty and the row loses the identity it was there to carry. AvatarFallback fills the same box with initials or an icon from first paint — it is what most users on poor connections actually see.

AccordionTrigger is itself the button inside the heading, and nesting a control within it is invalid, so the label has to be the trigger's own text. Without it the disclosure is announced as an unnamed button and a screen reader user has to open every section in turn to discover what each one holds.

Nested scroll containers fight over the same wheel and touch gestures: the inner region swallows the gesture until it reaches its own end, so the outer one reads as frozen and the content below it is unreachable by pointer. One region scrolls — restructure rather than stacking them.

Label wires nothing by itself: htmlFor is the only thing that turns its text into the control's accessible name, and an empty Label leaves the control nameless while looking finished on screen. Missing either, a screen reader announces the field as an unnamed edit box and clicking the caption does not focus it.

Activating a label activates the control it names, so a Button inside label text fires twice over: the click toggles the checkbox and runs the button's action. Buttons and links belong beside the label, never inside it; the control the label wraps is the one thing that may live there.

A Button's own text is its only accessible-name channel in this contract — aria-label is not among its declared props — so a Button emitted without text reaches the user as a control announced as nothing but "button". On a confirmation that is the difference between Cancel and the destructive action.

Select renders no control of its own. SelectTrigger is the focusable combobox and the element a Label's htmlFor must point at; SelectContent is the listbox holding the options. A Select missing either leaves nothing to focus, name, or open — only the aria-hidden native select Radix keeps in sync, which must never be labelled.

SelectValue is the only thing the trigger displays: the chosen item's label, or its placeholder while nothing is chosen. A trigger without one is a blank button, and a generated surface starts with nothing selected — so that placeholder text is the only thing naming what the field is asking for. A bare "Select..." names nothing.

A SelectContent holding no items is a listbox offering nothing to choose, and an option with no text is announced as an unnamed option, cannot be reached by typeahead, and leaves the trigger blank once chosen, because SelectValue echoes the item's own label. Subtree text admits items carrying an icon or a trailing Badge beside their label.

SelectGroup renders role=group and takes its accessible name from the SelectLabel inside it, from nowhere else. A group without one announces a boundary with no subject — the same confusion authors create by faking category headings with disabled items. SelectLabel is not the field's label; that is a separate Label bound to the trigger.

A RadioGroupItem outside a RadioGroup is inert — the group supplies the selection context and the roving tabindex. A group holding one item is worse: a checked radio cannot be unchecked, so the first arrow key or click commits a choice the user can never withdraw. A one-option question is a Checkbox or a Switch.

RadioGroupItem renders only its indicator and takes no children, so each option's text lives in a sibling Label bound to that item's id; a group of bare items is a column of radios announced with no option names. Held at should because the Field family's choice-card composition names options with FieldLabel, which this rule cannot see.

Controls that together answer one question — a checkbox group, a radio group, an address block — are named by the legend, which is announced with every control inside the set. A FieldSet whose legend is missing or empty announces a grouping with no subject, and a Label on one control names that control only, never the set.

FieldLabel is the only part of the family that names anything: Field generates no ids and wires nothing, FieldTitle is styled like a label but renders a div, and placeholder text is never a name. An empty FieldLabel leaves its control unnamed. Subtree text admits the choice-card composition, where the visible name is a FieldTitle inside the label.

Both families own the field's wiring and only one wins: FormControl stamps a generated id, aria-describedby, and aria-invalid onto the control it wraps, while Field expects those hand-written. Together they yield a duplicated id and an aria-describedby pointing at text that never renders. Field driven by Controller stays legal; the Form parts do not.

FormItem mints the id every other part derives from, FormControl stamps id, aria-describedby, and aria-invalid onto the control it wraps, and FormMessage is the element aria-describedby names once the field errors. A control outside FormControl receives none of that and still looks right on screen; a FormItem without one dangles.

FormLabel carries htmlFor bound to the id FormItem generated, so it is the field's name and a placeholder is not. A FormItem without one is a control whose label never renders; and any part placed outside a FormItem falls back to the id "undefined-form-item", collapsing every such field on the page onto one shared label.

Enter inserts a newline in a Textarea and does nothing on a Checkbox, Switch, or radio item, so a form whose controls are not single-line inputs has no keyboard path to submission — and with no Button, no pointer path either. Form is FormProvider and renders no DOM; the submit Button is the surface's only commit affordance.
A form-control represents the location of the user-editable control in a field. It must contain an approved interactive control; text-only or empty form controls are not meaningful form composition.

react.name: React
react.description: React components built with Radix UI primitives and styled with Tailwind CSS. Components are copied into your project source rather than imported from a package — you own and can modify the code.
react.guidance: Run 'npx shadcn@latest init' to set up the project, then add individual components with 'npx shadcn@latest add <component>'. Components are placed in your project (typically src/components/ui/ or components/ui/) and can be freely modified. Tailwind CSS v4 and a path alias (usually @/) are expected.

button.guidance: Uses class-variance-authority (cva) for variant styles. Supports Radix UI Slot via the asChild prop for composing with router Link components.

card.guidance: Pure HTML/CSS components — no Radix dependency.

input.guidance: A styled native <input> element. Forwards all standard HTML input attributes via React.forwardRef.

badge.guidance: Uses cva for variant styles. Renders as a <div> by default.

table.guidance: Pure HTML/CSS table primitives — no Radix dependency. Table renders a <table> wrapped in a horizontally scrollable container; the sub-components map directly to the native thead, tbody, tfoot, tr, th, td, and caption elements. The primitives are presentational only: sorting, filtering, pagination, and row selection are typically composed with TanStack Table (@tanstack/react-table) on top of them, where the headless library owns the data state and these components render the resulting rows and cells.
